usage_note: Replaced in federal law by "intellectual disability" (Rosa's Law, 2010). Recognize it in older records and state rules that still print it; don't use it in new writing.
basis: Rosa's Law, Pub. L. 111-256 (2010), as described in the ISBE Parent Guide (May 2025), p. 31; current federal term at 34 CFR 300.8(c)(6)

usage_note: The IDEA Amendments of 1997 dropped "serious" to remove its negative connotation; the federal term is "emotional disturbance", and some states (New York, for one) now say "emotional disability". Mental-health programs may still use the older phrase.
basis: IDEA Amendments of 1997, Pub. L. 105-17 (https://jan.ucc.nau.edu/~ldg/ese424/class/understanding/types/chart.html); current federal term at 34 CFR 300.8(c)(4)

usage_note: New Jersey's former term; its code now says "auditory impairment". Special-education law replaced "handicapped" with "disability" language when the federal law became the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1990.
basis: N.J.A.C. 6A:14-3.5(c)1, which says "auditory impairment" corresponds to "auditorily handicapped"; renaming of the federal law by the 1990 amendments (Future Reflections, NFB, Winter/Spring 1991, https://nfb.org/node/9224)
